newsitem.title: FRANCE: Grain markets cool but food debate rages on.
newsitem.headline: Grain markets cool but food debate rages on.

text.p: Grain farmers are gearing up for competition to sell from a bumper harvest only months after experts warned of dire shortages -- but pundits are split over whether the world still faces a longer-term food crisis.
Grain prices have dived since hitting records between April and July after unexpected increases in this year's crops.

Europe, Australia and Argentina are heading for near record grain harvests, the United States expects its fourth largest corn crop and import-giant China boasts this year's grain harvest will be its biggest yet.

Bigger crops have forced the European Union, the second largest wheat producer, to ditch a nine-month old policy of taxing exports to cope with scarcity. It now plans to revert to traditional export aid to fend of competition from overseas.
But with world consumption also rising, analysts say there will be room for only limited recovery in global grain reserves which are at 20-year lows this year after previous droughts.

"The American crop is better than we thought and Europe, Australia and Argentina are in excellent shape, but the recovery in stocks will be only very modest," a senior European grains executive said on Wednesday.

The International Grains Council, an authoritative London-based monitor, estimates world wheat output will rise 24 million tonnes to 563 million this year, but spare stocks will be just four million tonnes fatter at 101 million tonnes.

Nevertheless, many traders estimate that world wheat prices -- worth almost $300 a tonne in April -- will stabilise around the current $160 a tonne in coming months, easing inflation for cash-pinched importers and freeing up demand.
What happens then is still anyone's guess and sets free-marketeers and protectionists at each others' throats.
Lester Brown, president of the Washington-based Worldwatch Institute, leading the pessimists' camp, says scarcity will dominate grain in the years to come and force real prices up.
Speaking in London on Tuesday, he warned that China does not have enough land to sustain its current economic growth and lacks water to nourish crops.
"I don't believe anybody can supply China's needs," he said, forecasting imports would rise sharply as the country's 1.2 billion people switch to a more grain-intensive meat diet.
Brown dismissed the orthodox academic theory that historic grain yields will keep on rising as the world's agricultural machine runs faster.
But a British theorist snapped at the claims on Wednesday, alleging that Brown was in a long tradition of pessimism on world food supplies and had consistently been proved wrong.
"The market is more resilient than the pessimists think," Professor Alan Duncan of Oxford Policy Management wrote in a letter to the London-based Financial Times.
"A period of higher prices would, as we already see this year, cause resources to come back into grain production that were previously taken out as prices fell," he said.

Analysts say one of the unsolved riddles in the world's grain potential is the amount of land already in use in China itself. It is the largest producer of wheat for domestic consumption but statistics are often kept under a shroud.
Some Western analysts believe more land may already be under the plough in China than official figures suggest, implying that yields per acre are lower than thought and have room to go up.
New farm legislation in the United States, abolishing a raft of Depression-era farm subsidies, will also encourage farmers to respond to the market by growing as much they like, they say.
What most analysts bury their differences, however, is that grain demand is bound to keep rising for a few years yet, driven mainly by fast economic growth and changes in lifestyle in Asia.
The Grains Council sees total demand rising three percent to 1.4 billion tonnes this year, of which 558 million is for wheat.
